chunks.title: Who I am
chunks.text: Vineeth Reddy Kodakandla is an AI/ML engineer who builds AI systems that make it out of the notebook and into production. He recently completed an MS in Computer Science at Texas A&M University–Corpus Christi (2026). His work runs along two tracks. The first is agentic systems: giving LLMs memory, tools, and enough structure to act dependably instead of just impressively in a demo. The second is on-device inference and performance: quantizing models and measuring what they actually cost in latency, jitter and accuracy on real hardware, rather than trusting a vendor benchmark. He is targeting AI/ML Engineer, Applied AI, Inference/Performance Engineer, and Forward Deployed Engineer roles, and is open to relocating anywhere.

chunks.title: Project: ANANTA (agent memory that forgets on purpose)
chunks.text: ANANTA is Vineeth's agentic-memory project and the first piece of work featured on his site. It attacks a specific failure of most 'agent memory': a vector store that only ever grows, so retrieval quality decays as the corpus fills with stale facts. ANANTA models memory the way people do. An Ebbinghaus forgetting curve decays every memory over time, recall reinforces it in the manner of spaced repetition, and a periodic decay pass prunes what has faded. Every write is SHA-256 hash-chained into a tamper-evident audit log that a visitor can actively try to break in the live demo. On top of the memory layer sit two things: confidence-banded model routing, which escalates from memory to an 8B model to a 70B model to a frontier model only as confidence demands, and a Reflexion agent loop that runs plan, recall, retrieve via RAG, route, draft, self-check, then either answers or abstains. The abstain path is deliberate: it is built to decline rather than guess. It runs entirely in the browser with zero dependencies, and a visitor can supply their own Groq API key to get real model answers. Live demo: https://vineethkodakandla.github.io/ananta-lab/ — source: https://github.com/vineethkodakandla/ananta-lab. Stack: JavaScript, Web Crypto, RAG, model routing, Reflexion, zero-dependency.

chunks.title: Project: Edith (governed multi-agent orchestrator)
chunks.text: Edith is Vineeth's multi-agent orchestration project and the companion piece to ANANTA. Its argument is that most multi-agent demos are just agents chatting, which produces confident-sounding output nobody has checked. Edith is instead a governed team: an orchestrator dispatches specialists over a shared blackboard in a fixed pipeline — Researcher, which retrieves via RAG, then Analyst, then Critic, which runs a Reflexion self-critique pass, then Synthesizer. A Governor policy gate sits at the end and blocks any recommendation that is not grounded, hedged and actionable, sending it back for revision rather than releasing it. The behaviour Vineeth cares about most is what it does when it cannot answer: asked something off-corpus, it refuses to ship a confident guess and escalates for human review instead. Where ANANTA is about what a single agent remembers and forgets, Edith is about how a team of agents is governed, so the two are deliberately distinct rather than variations on one demo. Like ANANTA it is an interactive browser demo with zero dependencies, and a visitor can supply their own Groq API key for real model answers. Live demo: https://vineethkodakandla.github.io/edith-lab/ — source: https://github.com/vineethkodakandla/edith-lab. Stack: multi-agent orchestration, blackboard architecture, Reflexion, policy-gate governance, RAG, zero-dependency JavaScript.

chunks.title: Project: Meteor Lake Latency Lab (edge inference benchmarking)
chunks.text: The Meteor Lake Latency Lab is Vineeth's edge-inference and performance-engineering project, and the one that best shows his systems and measurement discipline rather than his agent work. It runs real-time instance segmentation (YOLOv8n-seg at 640x640) on an Intel Core Ultra 7 155H across all three processors that share the chip's package power budget — the NPU, the Arc integrated GPU, and the CPU — using OpenVINO, with INT8 post-training quantization via NNCF. A 33.3 ms per-frame budget (30 fps) was fixed before any measurement, and twelve configurations were scored pass/fail against it. The headline result is that the correct device depends on duty cycle: running inference back-to-back, the iGPU has the best median (11.3 ms) but a 47 ms p99, while the NPU holds an 18 ms p99; on a real 30 fps webcam the same iGPU configuration runs 10.4 ms median and 13.3 ms p99 and beats the NPU on both, because it idles roughly 70 percent of each frame interval. Measuring only the saturated case would have recommended the wrong processor. He also found the tail was not an inference problem at all: on the frames that missed the budget, inference time was normal while the CPU-side preprocess and postprocess stalled for 30 to 137 ms, and iGPU load produced 63 such stalls per 4000 frames against the NPU's 6. Rigor points he can speak to: calibration and evaluation sets are disjoint (COCO val2017 split 300/4700) so the INT8 accuracy is not flattered; his hand-written NumPy postprocess was verified against the reference implementation at 371 of 371 detections matching at IoU 0.9; two INT8 variants were built so the mixed-precision decision was measured rather than assumed, showing that excluding the detection-head decode costs 0.0015 box mAP while quantizing it costs 0.0389, 26 times more, for 0.35 ms. He is explicit about limits: power was never measured, and the stall mechanism is reported as unattributed because separating compositor contention from power droop would need tracing he did not do. Stack: Python, OpenVINO, NNCF, INT8 quantization, NPU/iGPU/CPU targeting, OpenCV, benchmarking and statistics. Live report: https://vineethkodakandla.github.io/edge-vision-lab/ — source: https://github.com/vineethkodakandla/edge-vision-lab

chunks.title: Project: bitwise-forensics (batch-dependent output changes in LLM serving)
chunks.text: bitwise-forensics is Vineeth's LLM-serving measurement project. It asks whether an inference engine returns the same tokens for a prompt when other requests share its engine steps, the kind of effect Thinking Machines described in 'Defeating Nondeterminism in LLM Inference'. He built a harness that serves 40 prompts alone and then together on Poisson arrival schedules, compares every run with the same prompt's batch-of-1 output token by token and on the chosen-token logprob, and reports where outputs fork, how far logprobs drift before they do, and paired bootstrap confidence intervals over prompts and trials. He measured a real engine, OpenVINO GenAI 2026.3's ContinuousBatchingPipeline serving Qwen2.5-Coder-0.5B-Instruct (INT4 weights) with greedy decoding, on the Arc iGPU and the CPU of an Intel Core Ultra 7 155H: 12 configurations per device, 40 prompts x 8 trials x up to 128 tokens, 7,680 runs in total on the same 40 prompts. Under default settings, sharing engine steps changed the tokens of 95.6 to 100 percent of iGPU runs and 54.4 to 72.5 percent of CPU runs. The engine was deterministic given the schedule: replaying the eight c8 arrival schedules under default options reproduced all 320 runs on each device bit for bit (tokens, chosen-token logprobs and per-token batch sizes), and batch-of-1 output was bitwise identical across two repeated passes and a pass served after the trials, for every option set. So the finding is not that inference is random or 'nondeterministic': where replay was tested, the output was a fixed function of the arrival schedule, and a different schedule could change it. On the CPU the main lever was dynamic activation quantization: at arrival rate c8, turning it off cut the share of runs with changed tokens from 71.2 to 21.2 percent. An f32 KV cache alone left that share unchanged within a wide interval (71.6 percent, +0.3 points, 95% CI -14.7 to +15.0), although on the same schedules it still changed which tokens came out. With both settings together, 0 of 320 runs had changed tokens at c8, and 0 of 320 at c32, within at most 128 tokens. That setting is still not batch-invariant, because chosen-token logprobs differed from batch-of-1 in every one of those runs, by up to 2.9e-5. On the iGPU no tested setting removed the token changes; an f16 KV cache lowered the c8 share to 51.2 percent. A 16-token per-step budget (max_num_batched_tokens=16, shared with decode tokens, so prompts are split across several steps) raised the CPU c8 share from 71.2 to 90.0 percent (+18.8 points, 95% CI +5.3 to +32.2). Forks landed on uncertain tokens, where the batch-of-1 choice had a median probability of about 0.25. Rigor he can speak to: a replay control; repeated batch-of-1 baselines plus one served after the trials, which detect drift that changes batch-of-1 output but not drift confined to batched steps; interleaved configurations so drift cannot line up with load; paired comparisons instead of eyeballing overlapping intervals; raw per-token results in the repo, with the report code and the analysis/ scripts that derive the README's intervals, replay checks and simulator table; and CI on Linux and Windows. The project began as a simulator; when a 12-seed check showed that the simulator's load trend and effect sizes changed with the synthetic model's seed, he kept it only as a pipeline test and published real-engine results instead. Limits he states plainly: one small model, one laptop, one engine, greedy decoding, and one set of 40 short templated prompts about inference topics (4 templates x 10 topics, 38 to 45 tokens with the chat template, no code). The results do not compare OpenVINO with vLLM or other engines, do not show that batched outputs are worse, and do not identify which operation causes the change. Source and results: https://github.com/vineethkodakandla/bitwise-forensics. Stack: Python, OpenVINO GenAI, continuous batching, NumPy, bootstrap statistics, pytest, GitHub Actions.

chunks.title: Project: PathwiseAI (network AIOps, most FDE-aligned)
chunks.text: PathwiseAI is a network operations / AIOps tool and Vineeth's most Forward-Deployed-Engineer-aligned project. Network operators normally react to SLA violations after they happen and write policy in raw NETCONF. PathwiseAI predicts SLA violations early using an LSTM model, lets operators write policy in plain English instead of NETCONF, and runs every change through a digital-twin layer that validates it before it touches the live network. It has a React/TypeScript operator dashboard and was benchmarked against Cisco, VMware, and Fortinet. It was built around a real operator's workflow, not just a model. Stack: Python, LSTM, React, TypeScript, NETCONF, digital twin.

chunks.title: Project: Pathfinders (full-stack CI/CD analytics)
chunks.text: Pathfinders is a full-stack CI/CD analytics platform with a FastAPI backend, a React frontend, Redis and TimescaleDB for time-series pipeline data, and automation through GitHub Actions. It demonstrates Vineeth's full-stack and MLOps/infrastructure breadth.

chunks.title: Research: rule-based multi-agent access control
chunks.text: Vineeth's graduate research, done as a graduate research assistant under faculty mentor Dr. Carlos Rubio-Medrano, built an ABAC/XACML multi-agent system: a deterministic, rule-based counterpart to LLM agents for cooperative access-control decisions. This gives him a strong instinct for where probabilistic LLM agents need guardrails — when to trust the model and when to constrain it.

chunks.title: Skills and stack
chunks.text: Agents & LLMs: LangGraph, CrewAI, RAG, Mem0, LoRA/QLoRA, evaluation and prompting. Inference & edge: OpenVINO, NNCF, INT8 post-training quantization, targeting NPU / integrated GPU / CPU backends, latency and jitter profiling, OpenCV. MLOps & infrastructure: Docker, Kubernetes, AWS, FastAPI, GitHub Actions, CI/CD. Languages: Python, TypeScript, SQL. Data & frontend: React, PostgreSQL, TimescaleDB, Redis. The inference and edge skills are demonstrated end to end in the Meteor Lake Latency Lab project rather than only listed: quantizing a segmentation model, targeting three different processors through one runtime, and reporting latency distributions and the accuracy cost honestly, including the limits of the study.

chunks.title: Teaching and assistantship experience
chunks.text: During his MS, Vineeth worked as a graduate/teaching assistant under Dr. Carlos Rubio-Medrano and teaching-assisted a Computer Forensics course. His graduate coursework included Computer Architecture, Advanced Software Engineering, Network Security, and Agent-Based Systems.

chunks.title: What I'm looking for
chunks.text: Vineeth is open to work and targeting AI/ML Engineer, Applied AI, and Forward Deployed Engineer roles. He is open to relocating anywhere. He is most interested in teams building products where models have to work in front of real users — production AI, not research demos.

chunks.title: How I think about engineering
chunks.text: Vineeth cares most about the seam where a model meets a real user and has to keep working. He values reliability, evaluation, and the unglamorous MLOps plumbing that turns a clever prototype into a system people can depend on. His research in deterministic rule-based systems informs how he adds guardrails around probabilistic LLM behavior.

chunks.title: FAQ: work authorization and sponsorship
chunks.text: Vineeth is authorized to work in the United States now. He is an F-1 student on OPT following his MS in Computer Science at Texas A&M University-Corpus Christi, so he can start without any action from an employer. Longer term he will need H-1B sponsorship to continue beyond OPT. He is happy to talk through timelines and specifics directly, and he would rather know early whether a team is able to sponsor than find out late in a process. Roles that require US citizenship or an active security clearance are not a fit.

chunks.title: FAQ: how to get in touch
chunks.text: The best way to reach Vineeth is by email (see the contact section of the site) or via LinkedIn. He responds to recruiters and engineers building production AI. Links to his GitHub, LinkedIn, and resume are in the site's contact section.
